newsitem.title: GREECE: Balkan foreign ministers push to end conflicts.
newsitem.headline: Balkan foreign ministers push to end conflicts.

text.p: Balkan foreign ministers on Tuesday urged Albania to hold free elections and the former Yugoslav republics to implement the Dayton peace deal.

Meeting in this northern Greek city to forge closer ties by developing political and economic cooperation, the ministers issued a joint declaration defining their European orientation and urging peace in the volatile area.
"The (ministers) underline the necessity of immmediately reinstituting internal peace and stability in Albania through the free will of the Albanian people," the declaration said.

It said the full implementation of the Dayton agreement, which ended civil war among the former Yugoslav states, would eliminate a major factor of instability in the region but there were still many steps to be taken.
"The (ministers) encourage all parties to the agreement to do their utmost for its full implementation...as soon as possible," the declaration said.
Ministers from Albania, Bulgaria, the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, Greece, Romania, Turkey and Serbia attended the two-day meeting of southeast European states which ends on Tuesday.

"The future of our area hinges on European unification. Each country must make its own steps towards this direction," Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos told a news conference. Greece is the only Balkan country member of the EU.

Balkan countries -- most emerging from decades of communism and facing harsh economic problems -- pledged to boost cooperation in the fields of energy, industry, banking and telecommunications, Pangalos said.
Despite their eagerness to leave behind a violent past and to improve their economies to EU standards, ministers did not hesitate to bring up festering political disputes.

Albania, which hopes elections on June 29 will help end the violence that erupted with the collapse of pyramid investment schemes earlier this year, complained about its large ethnic minority in the Serbian province of Kosovo.

"The situation in Kosovo continues to constitute a potential threat to regional security but...there are no signs of political will for a peaceful solution of the problem," Albanian deputy Foreign Minister Albert Rakipi said in his speech.

Greece clearly relished the low level of representation from Turkey, which sent an assistant deputy minister to the meeting. The two NATO members are at odds over a number of issues, including rights in the Aegean sea.
"We are surprised that Turkey did not evaluate this meeting correctly but it does give Greece more room to move," a Greek diplomat told Reuters.
